content:
FastTrackr wrote this. We're one of the tools compared.

Firms looking at advisor transition software often end up comparing FastTrackr, Docupace, Skience, Advisor360° and Laser App, even though they do different jobs. FastTrackr's column describes what our product does today. The other columns quote each vendor's own site, with the date we checked it. There's no score and no ranking. Which tool fits depends on the move, the custodian and who does the work.

"Not stated on the page we checked" means we didn't find it in the text of that vendor's page on 2026-11-04. It doesn't mean the product can't do it. Vendor quotes are the vendor's own claims, and we haven't verified them.

What each vendor says on its own site

Docupace's transitions page says "Move advisors to your firm in weeks, not months" and claims "500 advisors and 120,000 client accounts in 2025" (docupace.com, checked 2026-11-04). Those are Docupace's own claims.

Skience has a page called "Skience Advisor Transitions Solution" (skience.com, checked 2026-11-04). We couldn't read more of that page's text, so the Skience column is mostly blank rather than guessed.

Advisor360°'s account transitions update says its bulk onboarding handles "up to 6,000 accounts in 90 seconds" (advisor360.com, checked 2026-11-04).

Laser App, now under iPipeline, is a forms library. Its product page lists "33,000+ forms" (ipipeline.com, checked 2026-11-04). We didn't find transition-specific content there.

Questions to ask any vendor

  • Which custodians are live today, and which are still coming?
  • How does the paperwork go out: e-signature, filled PDFs for a wet signature, or the counterparty's own template?
  • What happens after the client signs? Who follows NIGO rejections and status updates until each account is done?
  • What can you start from? In a breakaway the old firm doesn't hand over an export, so it depends on your data access rights. In an acquisition the old firm hands over its exports.
  • Is it software you run, a team that runs it for you, or both?

When another tool fits better

  • If your book is moving to BNY Pershing now, Dispatch and Feathery both name Pershing on their transitions pages (checked 2026-11-04). FastTrackr's Pershing support is coming soon.
  • If you mainly need a large forms library rather than a transition workflow, Laser App lists 33,000+ forms (checked 2026-11-04).

How to build the business case with your own numbers

Build the case on your firm's figures, not a vendor's. Count these for the moves you ran last year, then for the ones you expect next year.

  • Revenue waiting on the move. Multiply the AUM in transition by your fee rate and divide by 365 to get a daily figure. Multiply that by the days accounts sit between custodians.
  • Staff time per move. Add up the hours spent preparing forms, submitting them, fixing NIGO rejections and chasing status. Multiply by the loaded hourly cost of the people doing it, including any temporary help.
  • Rework. Count the submissions that came back not in good order and how long each took to fix and resend.
  • Assets at risk. Take the AUM in motion, times your own attrition rate during past moves, times your fee rate.
  • Capacity. How many moves can your current team run at once before you have to hire?

Keep each input separate, so finance and operations can each check the part they own. Our cost of repapering calculator runs a similar estimate for labor, rework and delay.

What the workflow should connect

Most delays start in the data, the documents or the tracking. Separate tools can handle each one, but then someone re-keys data from one tool into the next, and that is where errors creep in. When you evaluate a tool, follow one account from start to finish:

  • Client data comes in once, from the documents and exports you actually have.
  • That data fills the forms the destination custodian and firm need for each account type.
  • Each form is checked against those requirements before it goes out.
  • After signing, each account is tracked, and a rejection goes to a named person the day it comes back.

Ask where a person still copies data by hand. And look at your own data first. Missing or inconsistent client details cause rejections whether forms are filled by software or by hand.

What to ask to see in a demo

  • A sample move run end to end, from the data you have to a tracked account.
  • The audit trail: who submitted each form, who approved it and when the client signed.
  • Status across every account in one move, and across several moves running at once.
  • The vendor's own figures on rejections and days to completion, and how they were measured.
  • How clients are kept informed during the move, and how often they will be contacted.

How to roll it out across offices

Firms with several offices do better when they start small and expand on results, not on a calendar date.

Start with a pilot

  • Pick one office with steady transition volume, but not your busiest.
  • Use the new tool only for moves that start during the pilot. Anything already submitted to a custodian finishes the old way.
  • Run the manual process alongside it at first, so any error gets caught.
  • Write down how you will judge it before you start: rejection rate against your current baseline, days to completion and staff hours per move.
  • Agree who can pause the pilot and what would make them do it.
  • Have compliance review the pilot's logs while it runs, not only at the end.

Expand on results

  • Agree on one set of compliance controls across offices before they go live. If you have more than one legal entity, map each entity's supervision first.
  • Check each office's custodian mix and confirm the tool covers it.
  • Give each office one person whose job is getting advisors and ops staff to use it.
  • Bring OSJ managers in early. A view of every move in progress gives them more oversight, not less.
  • Review rejections office by office. Error patterns often differ by office and by type of move.
  • Once results hold up, set a date after which every new move starts on the new tool.
